title: Multiple Assignment
summary: Declare several variables in one statement, chain assignments, and unpack or swap values with destructuring.
intro: Programs often need a few related values at once: the parts of a color, a set of counters, two values to swap. JavaScript gives you three tools for that: comma-separated declarations, chained assignment, and array destructuring.

steps.title: Several variables in one statement
steps.body:
One `let` or `const` can declare several variables. Separate each `name = value` pair with a comma and end the whole statement with one semicolon.

```javascript
let a = 1, b = 2, c = 3;
const x = 10, y = 20;
console.log(a, b, c, x, y); // 1 2 3 10 20
```

With `const`, every variable in the list is a constant. With `let`, every one can be reassigned later.

You can leave values out. A `let` declared without a value starts as `undefined` until you assign it. A `const` must always get a value right away.

```javascript
let first, last;
console.log(first); // undefined
```

JavaScript has no Python-style `a, b = 1, 2`. That line runs without an error but unpacks nothing: it only sets `b` to 1. Use a comma-separated declaration instead.

When the values are long, one declaration per line reads better:

```javascript
const title = "Hack University";
const motto = "Learn by building";
console.log(title, "-", motto); // Hack University - Learn by building
```

example.title: Color channels
example.prompt: Declare the red, green, and blue channels of orange in one statement and print them.
example.code:
const red = 255, green = 165, blue = 0;

console.log(red, green, blue);
example.explanation: One `const` statement creates three constants, each with its own value. `console.log` with three arguments prints them separated by single spaces.

practice.title: Box dimensions
practice.prompt:
Declare the three dimensions of a box in one statement and print them.

1. In one `const` statement, declare `width` as 30, `height` as 20, and `depth` as 10.
2. Print the text `Box:` followed by the three values, separated by single spaces.

Expected output:

```text
Box: 30 20 10
```
practice.starter:
// TODO: declare width, height, and depth in one const statement

// TODO: print Box: followed by the three values
practice.solution:
const width = 30, height = 20, depth = 10;

console.log("Box:", width, height, depth);
hints: Write `const` once, then the three `name = value` pairs separated by commas.
`console.log` can take the text `"Box:"` as its first argument and the three variables after it.

steps.title: Chained assignment
steps.body:
An assignment like `b = 0` is itself an expression whose value is `0`. That lets you chain assignments to give several variables the same value:

```javascript
let a, b, c;
a = b = c = 0;
console.log(a, b, c); // 0 0 0
```

Chains run from right to left: `c = 0` happens first, then `b` gets that result, then `a` does. Afterwards each variable holds its own number, so changing one later does not change the others.

Only chain variables you already declared. It is tempting to write `let x = y = 0;`, but that declares only `x`. The `y = 0` part assigns to a name that was never declared, and in a normal script file JavaScript silently creates a global variable called `y` instead of reporting an error. Declare every name first, then chain:

```javascript
let x, y;
x = y = 0;
console.log(x, y); // 0 0
```

Chain `let` variables only, since a `const` can never be assigned again.

example.title: Reset the scoreboard
example.prompt: Reset three counters to zero with one chained assignment, then record some wins.
example.explanation: The declaration leaves all three counters `undefined`. The chain sets `draws` to 0, then `losses`, then `wins`. Setting `wins` to 3 afterwards changes only `wins`, so the others stay at 0.

practice.title: Traffic light counters
practice.prompt:
Give three counters the same starting value with one chained assignment, then change one of them.

1. Declare `red`, `yellow`, and `green` with one `let` statement and no values.
2. Set all three to 5 with one chained assignment.
3. Change `yellow` to 2.
4. Print the three counters in the order red, yellow, green, separated by single spaces.

Expected output:

```text
5 2 5
```
hints: Declare the three names after one `let`, separated by commas, with no values.
Write the three names joined by `=` and put the value at the far right.
Change `yellow` on its own line after the chain, so the other two keep their value.

steps.title: Unpacking and swapping with destructuring

example.title: Podium and swap
example.prompt: Unpack two medal names, then swap two numbers with destructuring.
example.explanation: The first line copies `"gold"` into `first` and `"silver"` into `second`, matching by position. For the swap, the right side reads the current values into a temporary list `[2, 1]`, then the left side unpacks it, so `left` becomes 2 and `right` becomes 1. The semicolon after the `before:` line keeps the `[` line from joining it.

practice.title: Medals and rotation
practice.prompt:
Unpack three medal winners, then rotate three letters one step to the left.

1. Unpack `["Ada", "Bo", "Cy"]` into `gold`, `silver`, and `bronze` with one `const` destructuring statement.
2. Print the three winners separated by single spaces.
3. Rotate `a`, `b`, and `c` one step left with one destructuring assignment, so `a` gets the value of `b`, `b` gets the value of `c`, and `c` gets the value of `a`.
4. Print `a`, `b`, and `c` separated by single spaces.

Expected output:

```text
Ada Bo Cy
y z x
```

tests.output:
Ada Bo Cy
y z x

hints: Put the names in brackets on the left: `const [gold, silver, bronze] = ...;`
For the rotation, put `a`, `b`, and `c` in brackets on the left and list their new values on the right in the same order.
The right side reads all three old values before any assignment happens, so you need no temporary variable.

recap:
- `let a = 1, b = 2;` and `const x = 1, y = 2;` declare several variables in one statement.
- `let a, b;` declares variables that start as `undefined`.
- Use one declaration per line when values are long.
- `a = b = c = 0;` assigns from right to left. Chain only names you already declared, never `let x = y = 0;`.
- `const [x, y] = [3, 4];` unpacks values in order.
- `[a, b] = [b, a];` swaps two variables. A temporary variable works too.
- End every statement with a semicolon so a line starting with `[` or `(` never joins the line before it.
